I did a quick search to see if increased thermal mass in refridgerators improved efficiency..lots of questions, but few answers with proof.

Most of the info on increased efficiency focused on making the fridge run better. Having the coils on the back clean and having adequate room for air flow over them. Another probably big item was letting things cool before putting them in the fridge.

Now to look at the main question.. I'm thinking what a lot of people are thinking of is something like the thermal flywheel effect for buildings. The large mass of water in the fridge and freezer will protect against sudden oscillations of temperature change. Situations like opening the door and all the air rushing out/in and making the fridge turn on. Factors that affect are the amount of air exchanged, the energy gained by the fridge system by this air exchange, and this energy compared to the entire fridge system.

The thing I'm no sure about is because lots o fridges are an On/Off control how the increased thermal mass would affect the cooling cycle. Would the fridge be turning on many times during the cooling to work a lot to get the water cooled? How would that work overall on the efficiency?

I can appreciate having bottles of water in the freezer, because they require a lot of energy to heat up and that's helpful in power outages. Bottles of water in the fridge would be less useful. To heat 1kg of water, 1L or ≈ 0.25 Gallon, at 5°C ≈ 40F would take 4.4 kJ roughly. To melt 1 kg ≈2.2 lb of ice takes 334 kJ. So it'd be better to have more ice bottles in the freezer as you'd be able to keep things colder longer.

Or you could have something that melts/freezes just above your fridges top temperature range. That way when the power went out and your fridge began to heat up you'd have the material that would need to be thawed before heating could start. savE ® OM 05 from PLUSS® Melts at 4.5°C. Latent heat of fusion of 180 kJ/kg. So just over half the amount of energy to melt per kg than water.

Between 1915 and 1924, Henry Ford, Thomas Edison, Harvey Firestone, and John Burroughs, calling themselves the Four Vagabonds, embarked on a series of summer camping trips. The idea was initiated in 1914 when Ford and Burroughs visited Edison in Florida and toured the Everglades. These expeditions familiarized the public with the idea that automobiles could be used for recreation such as camping. After 1924, the growing fame of the campers brought too much public attention and the trips were discontinued.
